transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. I guess I came in because... well, I honestly can't see my studio or my life getting back on track anymore. I'm a carpenter, and it just feels like no matter how hard I work, or what kind of payment plan they put in front of me, it doesn't make a difference. I just don't see things ever getting any better.
How long have you been feeling this way — that things won't get better no matter what you do?
It's been going on since I took on the mortgage for the studio. That was a little over two years ago... probably about two years and two months now.
Before you took on the mortgage for the studio two years ago, had you ever experienced a period like this before where you felt hopeless and things seemed bleak?

No, not like this. I mean, sure, work gets tough or money gets tight sometimes, but... no. Before I signed for the place, I was actually doing alright. I never really felt this kind of... just total dead end before. It really all just started with that loan.

Besides feeling hopeless about the studio and finances, have you noticed changes in other areas of your life — like your sleep, your appetite, your energy level, or how you feel about things you used to enjoy?

Well, my energy is just... it's gone. I mean, by midmorning, my arms feel like I've been hauling lumber all day. And it doesn't matter if I spent the whole night in bed, I still wake up feeling completely wiped out. It makes it really hard to just push through the day—measuring, cutting, even just returning phone calls to clients. It takes everything I have just to get through the basics.
When you first took on that mortgage two years ago, did you feel this hopeless and exhausted right away, or did it gradually build up over weeks or months after you signed?

I'm not really sure, to be honest. It's hard to remember exactly how it went down back then. I don't know if it hit me all at once the day I signed the papers, or if it... you know, just kind of crept up on me over those first few months. It all just blurs together now. I just know that ever since I got tied to that loan, it's been like this.

If the mortgage and studio situation were somehow resolved tomorrow — say you sold the studio or the financial pressure went away — do you think you'd start feeling better, or at this point do you think you'd still feel this hopeless and exhausted even if that problem was gone?

I don't know. I really don't. It's hard to even imagine that happening right now. I'd like to think I'd feel better if the money stuff was gone, but... I honestly don't know if I would. It feels like this is just how I am now.

In the months right before you took on that mortgage — say, the 3 to 6 months before you signed the papers — how was your mood back then? Were you feeling pretty good about things, or were you already struggling with low mood or hopelessness?

I'm not really sure. It's been a couple of years now, and it's hard to remember what things were like before all this started. I don't recall if I was already feeling down back then or if it was just the normal stress of getting ready to open the business. I just know it's been bad for a long time now.

Over these past two years, have there been any periods — even a few weeks or a month — where you felt noticeably less hopeless or had more energy, or has it been pretty consistently this bad the whole time?

No, I don't think so. It's... it's just been pretty much this bad the whole time. I can't really think of a week or even a few days where I felt any lighter or had more energy. It just feels like one long, heavy stretch ever since this all started.

When you think about your life before the mortgage — your work, your relationships, your day-to-day life — were you generally satisfied and able to enjoy things, or do you remember struggling with low mood or emptiness even back then?

I really can't say for sure. Honestly, it's just a blur. I don't remember if I was happy or just going through the motions back then. I mean, I was working, doing my carpentry, seeing people... but I don't know if I was actually enjoying it or if I was already feeling empty. It's just hard to separate it all out now. Everything just feels overshadowed by how bad it's been the last couple of years.

Looking back now, in those months right before you took on the mortgage, did you ever have stretches where you felt sad, empty, or down on yourself — independent of any worries about the business or money? Or was your mood pretty stable until after you signed the papers?

I... I really just don't remember. Like I said, it's all a blur before the mortgage. I don't know if I was sad or down on myself, or if I was fine. I just can't remember how I felt back then, before everything got so heavy.

I know it's hard to remember, but let me ask it this way: In the months right before you signed that mortgage, did you notice any sadness, emptiness, or loss of interest in things — even small things like hobbies or time with friends — before the financial stress of the loan kicked in?

I know you're trying to figure out if this all started before the money stress kicked in. I... I really wish I could give you a straight answer. But honestly, I just don't know. 

When I try to picture myself back then, doing my woodwork or seeing buddies... I just draw a blank on how I actually felt inside. It's like my mind just won't let me see past the last couple of years. I just don't have a clear memory of it to tell you one way or the other.

When you first signed those mortgage papers, did you feel the hopelessness and exhaustion hit you pretty quickly—like within days or a week or two—or did it take several months of dealing with the loan before you started feeling this way?

I think... I think it took a little while. It wasn't right away. When I first signed, I was just focused on the work, trying to get things going. But then, as the months went by and the reality of the payments and the pressure started to set in... that's when it really hit me. It just kind of piled up over several months until I was just completely worn out and feeling like there was no way out.

When you think back to the months right before you signed that mortgage—say, 6 months before—did you ever have days where you felt sad or down in mood, even if you're not sure why, or do you feel confident that you were doing okay emotionally back then?

Doc, I... it's just like I said a minute ago. I really don't know. I can't tell you I'm confident I was doing fine back then, and I can't say for sure I was down, either. Six months before the loan... it's just empty when I try to look back. I just honestly don't remember how I was feeling.

Let me ask it differently: In the weeks right after you signed that mortgage—say, the first month or two—did you notice the hopelessness and exhaustion starting to build, or were you still feeling basically normal at that point?

I think... I was still feeling basically normal then. The first month or two, I was just working, trying to keep up. The heavy stuff, the exhaustion... I didn't really notice that building up until later on.

When you think back to the first few months after you signed that mortgage—let's say months 2 through 6—that's when you started noticing the exhaustion and hopelessness building up, correct? And before that first month or two, you're saying you were still feeling basically okay?

Yeah, that sounds about right. The first couple of months, I was just... working, you know? Just doing what I had to do. I felt fine, or at least normal enough. It was after that, maybe three or four months in, when the weight of it all really started dragging me down. That's when the exhaustion and the... the feeling like I was trapped just sort of took over.

In those months before you took on the mortgage, did anyone close to you—like family or friends—ever mention that you seemed down, withdrawn, or different in mood or energy? Or did people seem to notice a change in how you were doing?

No, not that I can remember. Nobody said anything like that to me. I mean, I mostly just kept to myself and went to work, but my wife or the guys on the crew... they never mentioned me acting different or looking down before the mortgage. If they noticed anything, they didn't say a word to me about it.

Think back to the year before you took on that mortgage. During that entire year, would you say your overall mood and energy were pretty good, or do you recall having stretches of feeling down or low on energy for no particular reason?

I'd say... I was pretty good. Yeah, that whole year before we bought the house, my mood and energy were fine. I was just working my regular shifts, coming home, doing the usual stuff. I don't remember having any stretches where I felt down or exhausted like I do now. It was just a normal year for me.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient had depressive symptoms present before the mortgage stress began, which would support F32.9 (Major Depressive Disorder) over F43.20 (Adjustment Disorder). The key differentiator is whether this is a primary mood disorder with insidious onset that predates the stressor, or a reactive adjustment disorder directly triggered by the mortgage.
doctor.question: Think back to the year before you took on that mortgage. During that entire year, would you say your overall mood and energy were pretty good, or do you recall having stretches of feeling down or low on energy for no particular reason?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's mood and energy levels during the year *before* taking on the mortgage (which was over 2 years ago). patient.answer: I'd say... I was pretty good. Yeah, that whole year before we bought the house, my mood and energy were fine. I was just working my regular shifts, coming home, doing the usual stuff. inference.note: Ruled out F43.20 (Adjustment Disorder). Patient reports year of good mood/energy before mortgage, then normal first 1-2 months after signing, with gradual onset of hopelessness and exhaustion over months 3-6 onward—totaling 2+ years of persistent depressive symptoms. This timeline and presentation (insidious onset independent of initial stressor, persistent course, vegetative symptoms, anhedonia) is more consistent with Major Depressive Disorder than with Adjustment Disorder, which requires closer temporal relationship to identifiable stressor and typically resolves within 6 months of stressor onset or removal.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with a two-year history of persistent depressed mood, hopelessness, and fatigue that began several months after taking on a mortgage for his carpentry studio. The patient reports consistent low mood and energy without significant periods of remission. The year prior to the stressor showed normal mood and energy. Current presentation meets criteria for Major Depressive Disorder, single episode, unspecified severity (F32.9), as the two-year duration, persistent nature, and functional impairment in work capacity are documented.
